newsitem.title: USA: DRI/McGraw Hill says China bank problem "enormous".
newsitem.headline: DRI/McGraw Hill says China bank problem "enormous".

text.p: China's troubled banking sector represents one of the most serious threats to global market stability, economic forecasting firm DRI/McGraw Hill said Tuesday.

China's banking problem is "enormous," DRI/McGraw Hill said in a survey of the world's biggest emerging markets. Within the next three to five years, China could default on between 20 percent and 40 percent of the country's $600 billion in outstanding loans, it added.

"... The risk of (China's) serious debt problem will continue to mount and could have major economic ramifications for many of China's smaller and weaker economic neighbours," said the report titled "Country Risk Review."

Chinese banks have been crippled by government policies that force them to make questionable loans to state-owned or state-sponsored companies, many of which are in very weak financial positions, the report said.
DRI/McGraw Hill made its comments on China as it ranked the relative investment risk of the world's big emerging markets.
A number of financial analysts took issue with McGraw Hill's assessment of China's banking sector, however, saying the report overstated the implications for the world economy.

"It's absolutely false and incredibly misleading," said Chase Manhattan Bank Vice President Robert Visek. "This is still one of the fastest growing economies in the world. China will outgrow its problems."

Visek said banking problems have nothing to do with the risk of a foreign investor doing business in the country. He added that foreign banks doing business in China were increasing their loan portfolios by 40 percent to 50 percent a year.

"If the banks don't go bankrupt and the government does not go bankrupt, then what is the negative for the world economy?" Visek said, adding that the state-owned sector was shrinking as a proportion of China's overall economy.
Among the 10 countries surveyed, South Africa presented the highest investment risk due to a declining rate of growth and rising unemployment and inflation.
South Africa's mineral and agricultural output is stagnant or falling and consumer debt has reached dangerous proportions, the report said.

While South Africa recently had its sovereign debt rating upgraded and has increased its foreign reserves, "the general dismal fundamentals of the South African government and economy are expected to lead to poor long-term prospects" for the country, it added.
After South Africa and China, the report listed Indonesia, Russia and Brazil, in descending order, as having the highest investment risk.
Argentina, Poland, Mexico, Turkey and India offered the lowest investment risk among the biggest emerging markets, the report said.
